justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish but essentially flat trajectory from the current price level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing market price with only a slight upward drift, reflecting the general tendency for short-term price continuity in liquid equity or index instruments. The one-week and one-month estimates step up only marginally, capturing a modest positive drift consistent with historical equity risk premia while acknowledging that no strong directional catalyst was evident at the time of the forecast. The gradual upward slope across horizons is more a reflection of expected-value arithmetic than a strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a straightforward consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, realized volatility for most equity instruments tends to be relatively contained, so a roughly ±5 point band captures the bulk of plausible outcomes. By one week, intraday noise accumulates across multiple sessions and macro data releases become relevant, widening the band to roughly ±11 points. At one month, earnings cycles, central bank communications, and broader macroeconomic trends all come into play, pushing the 90% interval to roughly ±20 points. These widths were calibrated against typical historical volatility for an instrument trading near 200, implying an annualized volatility in the 15–20% range.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as an unexpected jump in unemployment claims, a hawkish central bank pivot, or a geopolitical shock — could easily drive prices below the lower bounds, particularly at the weekly and monthly horizons. Liquidity events or sudden shifts in market sentiment, sometimes triggered by large institutional positioning or options expiration dynamics, could also create outsized moves that historical volatility alone would not predict. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of prevailing geopolitical tensions could propel prices meaningfully above the upper bounds.

It is worth being transparent that these intervals, while quantitatively derived, carry their own model uncertainty. The assumption of roughly log-normal returns with stable volatility is a simplification; in practice, return distributions have fat tails, and volatility itself is time-varying and can spike suddenly. Events that fall in the tails of the distribution — by definition rare but not negligible — are precisely what my stated 10% combined tail probability is meant to account for. Readers should treat the intervals as reasonable probabilistic guidance rather than hard boundaries, and remain alert to regime changes that could render the underlying volatility assumptions obsolete.
